plan.contextChunk: This figure shows a uniform thin disk twice, in two side-by-side views. The left view looks straight down the rotation axis: a blue-shaded circle with x pointing up, y pointing right, and z labeled at the center where the axis emerges from the page. A double-headed arrow from center to outer edge is labeled R, a second arrow labeled r reaches a thin orange ring concentric with the rim, and a short arrow labeled dr points at that ring's width. The right view redraws the disk in oblique perspective as a shaded ellipse with an orange rim, z vertical, y to the right, x coming toward the lower left; a curved arrow loops around z to show the sense of rotation, and an arrow labeled r runs from the center to an element on the ring labeled dm. Showing the ring face-on and in perspective ties the annular strip of width dr to the mass element dm at one distance from the axis. The pairing motivates finding the moment of inertia by summing thin rings, each carrying all its mass at radius r.

interactionPlan.concept: The moment of inertia of a uniform disk is built by summing thin concentric rings, each of which carries all of its mass dm at a single distance r from the rotation axis, so its contribution is r² dm.
elements: Left panel: face-on view of the disk, looking down the rotation axis
Left panel: large blue-to-white radially shaded filled circle representing the uniform disk of radius R, thin blue-grey outline
Left panel: vertical axis arrow labeled 'x' pointing up, horizontal axis arrow labeled 'y' pointing right, both drawn through the disk center
Left panel: 'z' label at the center marking the axis emerging out of the page
Left panel: orange annulus (ring) concentric with the rim, drawn at radius r with visible width dr
Left panel: double-headed black arrow from center to outer rim labeled 'R' (drawn toward lower-left)
Left panel: arrow from center to the orange ring labeled 'r' (drawn toward lower-right)
Left panel: short arrow with label 'dr' pointing at the radial width of the orange ring (upper-right)
Right panel: oblique perspective view of the same disk drawn as a shaded ellipse with an orange rim
Right panel: vertical axis arrow labeled 'z' through the center, horizontal axis arrow labeled 'y' to the right, oblique axis arrow labeled 'x' toward the lower left
Right panel: curved arrow looping around the z axis indicating the sense of rotation
Right panel: arrow from center out to a point on the ring labeled 'r'
Right panel: small marker on the ring labeled 'dm' (the mass element)
Right panel: orange elliptical annulus matching the left panel's ring radius and width
Readout panel: current r/R, dr/R, ring area dA = 2πr dr, ring mass dm = (M/πR²)·dA, and contribution r² dm
Accumulation bar / running-total indicator for ΣI = Σ r² dm approaching ½MR²
Legend: orange = highlighted differential ring, blue = rest of the disk

interactions.label: Ring radius r / R
interactions.teaches: Moving the same ring outward increases its contribution r² dm sharply, because both the ring's circumference (its mass) and the lever-arm squared grow with r.

interactions.label: Ring width dr / R
interactions.teaches: The ring is a differential element: as dr shrinks, its mass dm shrinks proportionally and every point in it sits at essentially the same radius r, which is what makes r² dm exact.

interactions.label: View
interactions.teaches: The face-on circle and the tilted ellipse are the same object: the integration element is a complete ring encircling the rotation axis, not a point or a radial strip.

interactions.label: Sum rings from center to rim
interactions.teaches: Stacking every ring from r = 0 to r = R fills the whole disk and the accumulated Σ r² dm converges to I = ½MR², with most of the total arriving from the outer rings.

demo_steps.title: The whole disk
demo_steps.narration: A uniform disk of mass M and radius R spins about the z axis through its center. Seen face-on the axis points out of the page; seen in perspective the curved arrow shows the sense of rotation.

demo_steps.title: Pick one thin ring
demo_steps.narration: Highlight a single thin annulus at radius r with width dr. In the perspective view the same ring carries the mass element dm, and every bit of that mass sits at the same distance r from the axis.

demo_steps.title: Make the ring differential
demo_steps.narration: Shrink dr. The ring's area 2πr dr and its mass dm shrink with it, and the spread of radii inside the ring vanishes — this is why dI = r² dm is exact for a ring, not an approximation.

demo_steps.title: Slide the ring inward
demo_steps.narration: Near the center the ring is short, holds little mass, and its lever arm is tiny, so its r² dm contribution is almost nothing.

demo_steps.title: Slide the ring outward
demo_steps.narration: Push the same-width ring out to the rim: it is now long, holds far more mass, and each gram sits at the largest possible radius, so the contribution jumps dramatically.

demo_steps.title: Sum all the rings
demo_steps.narration: Add rings from the center out to R. They tile the entire disk, and the running total Σ r² dm climbs steeply only in the last part of the sweep, converging on I = ½MR².

interactionPlan.keyInsight: A ring is the natural mass element for a disk because all of its mass lies at one radius — and since that mass grows like r while the lever arm counts as r², the outer rings dominate the moment of inertia.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Two side-by-side panels on a white background. Left: a large circle with a soft blue-to-white radial/linear gradient fill and thin grey-blue outline, centered on crossed thin black axis arrows — 'x' up, 'y' right, italic 'z' labeled at the center. A concentric orange ring (stroke ~orange/salmon, fill lightly tinted) sits inside it; a double-headed black arrow from center to rim toward the lower-left labeled 'R'; a single arrow from center to the orange ring toward the lower-right labeled 'r'; a short arrow in the upper-right pointing inward at the ring's thickness labeled 'dr'. Right: the same disk drawn as a wide, flattened ellipse (oblique view) with the same blue gradient fill and an orange rim; a vertical 'z' arrow through the center, a 'y' arrow to the right, an 'x' arrow going down-left out of the plane; a small curved arrow circling the top of the z axis for rotation sense; a straight arrow from center to a point on the ring labeled 'r', with a small dot on the ring labeled 'dm'. All labels italic serif, matching the textbook style. Highlighted annulus in both panels must stay synchronized to the r and dr sliders. Below or beside the figure place a compact readout: r/R, dr/R, dA = 2πr dr, dm, and a horizontal bar whose length tracks r² dm, plus a second bar for the accumulated Σ r² dm scaled against ½MR². When the integrate button runs, previously summed rings stay drawn in faded orange so the learner sees the disk filling in from the center outward.

authoredContext:
Integrating to find the moment of inertia of a two-dimensional object is a little bit trickier, but one shape is commonly done at this level of study—a uniform thin disk about an axis through its center (the figure).

Calculating the moment of inertia for a thin disk about an axis through its center.

Figure shows a uniform thin disk of radius r that rotates about a Z axis that passes through its center.

Since the disk is thin, we can take the mass as distributed entirely in the xy-plane. We again start with the relationship for the surface mass density, which is the mass per unit surface area. Since it is uniform, the surface mass density σ is constant:

discrepancies: Right (perspective) panel: in the source only the ellipse rim is orange with the r arrow reaching the rim where dm sits; the generated version adds an inner orange annulus band and places the dm dot at r≈0.55R inside the disk, so the rim-mass-element reading of the original is altered.

Left panel: the source shows a thin orange circle (outline only) at radius r; the generated version draws a filled translucent orange annulus band — conceptually reasonable but visually heavier than the source's single stroked circle.

A large readout/legend panel with progress bars, dA/dm/dI text and colour swatches is appended below the figure; it has no counterpart in the source and its ~11 px text renders very small at inline size.
In the readout strip the right-hand caption text ('vs. same-width ring at the rim', '0% of ½MR² = 0.5 MR²') crowds into the legend swatches/labels at x≈620, producing mild collisions.
The curved rotation arrow above the z axis is smaller and flatter than in the source, and the source's larger sweeping loop is less legible here.
Overall canvas (900×560) leaves a large empty band under the figure and shrinks all glyphs when scaled to the inline container.
evaluation.notes: Both panels of the source are faithfully reproduced with correct axes, ring, and dr/r/R/dm labels, and the interaction set (radius/width sliders, view selector, ring-summation animation, 6 demo steps) is rich and physically correct; the main weaknesses are the extra dense readout panel with small, slightly colliding text and the inner-annulus treatment of the perspective panel that departs from the source's rim-only dm.

Tighten the viewbox height (or reflow the readout beside the figure) to remove the empty band below the artwork and let the two panels render larger.
Enlarge the curved rotation arrow above the z axis to match the source's wider sweep and give it a clearer arrowhead.

Accumulation bar / running-total indicator for ΣI = Σ r² dm approaching ½MR²
Legend: orange = highlighted differential ring, blue = rest of the disk

interactions.label: Ring radius r / R
interactions.teaches: Moving the same ring outward increases its contribution r² dm sharply, because both the ring's circumference (its mass) and the lever-arm squared grow with r.

interactions.label: Ring width dr / R
interactions.teaches: The ring is a differential element: as dr shrinks, its mass dm shrinks proportionally and every point in it sits at essentially the same radius r, which is what makes r² dm exact.

interactions.label: View
interactions.teaches: The face-on circle and the tilted ellipse are the same object: the integration element is a complete ring encircling the rotation axis, not a point or a radial strip.

interactions.label: Sum rings from center to rim
interactions.teaches: Stacking every ring from r = 0 to r = R fills the whole disk and the accumulated Σ r² dm converges to I = ½MR², with most of the total arriving from the outer rings.

demo_steps.title: The whole disk
demo_steps.narration: A uniform disk of mass M and radius R spins about the z axis through its center. Seen face-on the axis points out of the page; seen in perspective the curved arrow shows the sense of rotation.

demo_steps.title: Pick one thin ring
demo_steps.narration: Highlight a single thin annulus at radius r with width dr. In the perspective view the same ring carries the mass element dm, and every bit of that mass sits at the same distance r from the axis.

demo_steps.title: Make the ring differential
demo_steps.narration: Shrink dr. The ring's area 2πr dr and its mass dm shrink with it, and the spread of radii inside the ring vanishes — this is why dI = r² dm is exact for a ring, not an approximation.

demo_steps.title: Slide the ring inward
demo_steps.narration: Near the center the ring is short, holds little mass, and its lever arm is tiny, so its r² dm contribution is almost nothing.

demo_steps.title: Slide the ring outward
demo_steps.narration: Push the same-width ring out to the rim: it is now long, holds far more mass, and each gram sits at the largest possible radius, so the contribution jumps dramatically.

demo_steps.title: Sum all the rings
demo_steps.narration: Add rings from the center out to R. They tile the entire disk, and the running total Σ r² dm climbs steeply only in the last part of the sweep, converging on I = ½MR².

plan.keyInsight: A ring is the natural mass element for a disk because all of its mass lies at one radius — and since that mass grows like r while the lever arm counts as r², the outer rings dominate the moment of inertia.
plan.reconstructionNotes: Two side-by-side panels on a white background. Left: a large circle with a soft blue-to-white radial/linear gradient fill and thin grey-blue outline, centered on crossed thin black axis arrows — 'x' up, 'y' right, italic 'z' labeled at the center. A concentric orange ring (stroke ~orange/salmon, fill lightly tinted) sits inside it; a double-headed black arrow from center to rim toward the lower-left labeled 'R'; a single arrow from center to the orange ring toward the lower-right labeled 'r'; a short arrow in the upper-right pointing inward at the ring's thickness labeled 'dr'. Right: the same disk drawn as a wide, flattened ellipse (oblique view) with the same blue gradient fill and an orange rim; a vertical 'z' arrow through the center, a 'y' arrow to the right, an 'x' arrow going down-left out of the plane; a small curved arrow circling the top of the z axis for rotation sense; a straight arrow from center to a point on the ring labeled 'r', with a small dot on the ring labeled 'dm'. All labels italic serif, matching the textbook style. Highlighted annulus in both panels must stay synchronized to the r and dr sliders. Below or beside the figure place a compact readout: r/R, dr/R, dA = 2πr dr, dm, and a horizontal bar whose length tracks r² dm, plus a second bar for the accumulated Σ r² dm scaled against ½MR². When the integrate button runs, previously summed rings stay drawn in faded orange so the learner sees the disk filling in from the center outward.
